strengths: The paper addresses a clear and timely gap: current LLM-based 3D generators either produce coarse proxies or rely on external diffusion modules, and CG-MLLM is among the first attempts at native, end-to-end, high-resolution 3D generation inside an MLLM with joint understanding.

The mode-based binding of MoT transformers (TokenAR for serial tokens, BlockAR for parallel blocks) rather than task-based binding is a sensible and somewhat novel architectural idea, and the hybrid masking scheme with 3D-aware positional encoding (permutation invariance within blocks) is well motivated.

Empirically, the paper is fairly thorough for its size: it reports the best results among MLLM-based 3D generators (Tab. 1), demonstrates that 3D generation training transfers back to image-based 3D captioning (Tab. 2), and provides five ablation groups (Tab. 3) plus training/inference cost scaling analyses (Tabs. 4-5).

The paper is commendably honest: it explicitly acknowledges falling short of non-MLLM SOTA (TRELLIS, Hunyuan3D-2.1), reports the weak captioning-quality issue in its training data, documents failure modes, and includes two useful negative results (AdaLN instability in MLLMs, VAE reconstruction artifacts with importance-point sampling).

The observed perception gain from generation training (Qwen3-VL-2B: 3.13/7.21/11.92 vs. Ours-2B: 13.51/19.13/14.28 on captioning metrics) is an interesting finding supporting the unified-modeling hypothesis.
weaknesses: Key methodological details are under-specified. The paper motivates rectified flow at length (Sec. 2.2, including equations) but never clearly states how continuous 3D VAE latents are predicted inside the BlockAR transformer, what the 3D decoding head looks like, or how the '50 sampling steps' and CFG at inference relate to the BlockAR formulation. The connection between the flow-matching background and the actual generation mechanism must be inferred rather than stated, which harms reproducibility.

Presentation is rough in places: standalone subsections 4.3 ('Limitations of AdaLN in MLLM') and 4.4 ('VAE Reconstruction Issues') interrupt the experiments flow; the 'DeepStack' component in Fig. 1 is not explained in the figure or text; Fig. 3 masks are described only at a high level; and the text-to-3D and 3D-input understanding modes shown in Fig. 2 are never quantitatively evaluated.

Evaluation strength is uneven. Generation comparisons are limited to two MLLM baselines (SAR3D, ShapeLLM-Omni), and the captioning comparison (Tab. 2) pits a 2B model against outdated 13B baselines (InstructBLIP, LLaVA-13B) while conceding a large gap to 3D-LLM/PointLLM/ShapeLLM-Omni; the 'outperforms Qwen3-VL' claim rests on a single weak baseline. The user study covers only ~100 questionnaires / 2,400 data points, and no code or model release is mentioned, limiting reproducibility.

The core claim of 'high-resolution' 3D generation is undercut by the paper's own limitations section: fewer than 4k tokens are used versus up to 10x more in competing methods, the VAE/processing pipeline is borrowed from Hunyuan3D-2.1, and the authors concede overall quality falls short of commercial and non-MLLM systems. The contribution is thus 'best among a weak MLLM class' rather than an advance over the broader state of the art.

The architecture is heavily assembled from existing components (Qwen3-VL, Hunyuan3D-2.1 VAE, MoT, rectified flow), so the marginal novelty is concentrated in the TokenAR/BlockAR masking and mode-binding design; the paper would benefit from more direct evidence that this specific design (e.g., vs. a single-transformer hybrid mask or Transfusion-style baseline) is what drives the gains, beyond the coarse MOT on/off ablation.

strengths: Genuinely interesting research direction: CG-MLLM is, to the authors' knowledge, among the first MLLMs to perform end-to-end 3D asset generation natively (via flow matching on VAE latents within a hybrid causal/parallel masking scheme) rather than delegating to an external diffusion generator, and the perception-transfer observation (Table 2) is a worthwhile finding.

The paper is refreshingly honest in places: it concedes that it does not surpass state-of-the-art non-MLLM methods, devotes a full limitations section with concrete failure cases (Fig. 8), and reports negative results on AdaLN (Sec. 4.3) and VAE point-sampling (Sec. 4.4).

The efficiency analysis is useful: Tables 4 and 5 quantify training/inference scaling with 3D-token budget, and the claimed ~3x speedup of block-parallel over token-level decoding is practically relevant.
Ablation Table 3 is reasonably informative, showing that the MoT design, the stronger VAE, and the larger token budget each contribute, and that performance follows a scaling trend across backbones.
weaknesses: The central contribution is largely an integration of existing components (Qwen3-VL, Hunyuan3D-2.1 VAE, Mixture-of-Transformers, rectified flow, DeepStack). The method section mostly restates these components; the genuinely novel design decisions (hybrid masking, binding transformers to generation modes rather than tasks) are described qualitatively but never ablated in isolation—e.g., there is no comparison against a single-transformer hybrid-masking variant or against a task-binding MoT baseline.

Key claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The abstract promises 'high-resolution 3D generation,' yet Sec. 5 admits the reconstruction uses fewer than 4k tokens while current high-resolution methods need up to 10x more, and the paper concedes it does not comprehensively surpass non-MLLM baselines (p-FID 12.55 vs. TRELLIS 7.36). Similarly, the claim of 'superior spatial reasoning / outperforming Qwen3-VL in 3D understanding tasks' rests only on captioning BLEU/ROUGE/METEOR on image inputs, a narrow proxy for 3D understanding with no spatial QA or reasoning benchmarks.

Comparisons in Tables 1 and 2 are confounded by differing training data, VAEs, rendering pipelines, and model scales (e.g., a 2B model compared against 7B/13B captioning models), and the paper does not control for these factors, weakening the SOTA-among-MLLMs claim. The user study is small (~100 questionnaires, ~2,400 judgments) with no details on participant selection or protocol.

Reproducibility is poor: dataset sizes, filtering details, total token counts, stage durations, and the full training recipe are not specified, and there is no code, model, or data release mentioned. Given the pipeline depends on bespoke curation of LLaVA-OneVision, Trellis-500K, and Objaverse++ with Hunyuan3D preprocessing, others cannot reliably rebuild the system.

Presentation issues further reduce confidence: several references are incomplete (missing years/venues, e.g., Fang et al., Zhao et al., Li et al.), typos ('uniformly points', 'captioning evaluation' results in Fig. 7 are asserted but the captioning benchmark it references is unclear), and Fig. 3's mask heatmaps are hard to interpret at the printed scale.

The ablation in Table 3 changes multiple factors simultaneously across rows (VAE, MoT, backbone, token budget), so the individual contribution of the architectural novelty (MoT with BlockAR) versus simply a better VAE and backbone is not cleanly isolated; the Qwen2.5-0.5B row with neither VAE nor MoT (p-FID 53.66) is a weak point of comparison.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely gap: bringing native, end-to-end high-resolution 3D generation into the MLLM paradigm, whereas prior LLM-based 3D models (SAR3D, ShapeLLM-Omni) produce only coarse proxies or tokenized meshes. The quantitative results (Table 1: p-FID 12.55, p-KID 0.27) show a meaningful improvement over prior MLLM-based 3D generation methods.

The architectural design—binding TokenAR and BlockAR transformers to generation modes (serial vs. parallel) rather than to tasks—is a sensible and clearly articulated evolution of Mixture-of-Transformers, and Section 3.4 provides a thoughtful comparison against related MoT-based methods (LMFusion, Transfusion-style approaches).

The ablation studies (Table 3) are reasonably comprehensive, covering the VAE backbone, the MoT architecture, the LLM backbone, token budget, and scaling behavior, and they support the claim that the method follows a scaling-law trend. The training/inference cost tables (Tables 4-5) aid reproducibility and practical assessment.

The paper is refreshingly honest about limitations: it acknowledges it does not surpass state-of-the-art non-MLLM methods, reports failure cases (Fig. 8), discusses the data preprocessing pipeline's precision loss, and includes useful negative results (AdaLN being suboptimal in MLLMs; the VAE importance-point sampling issue in Sec. 4.4).

The observation that learning 3D generation transfers back to perception (Table 2, image-input captioning improving dramatically over Qwen3-VL-2B) is an interesting and potentially valuable finding beyond generation itself.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely compositional: the system combines a pretrained Qwen3-VL backbone, a frozen Hunyuan3D-2.1 VAE, and the MoT architecture with adapted masking. The core ideas (hybrid causal/parallel masking, dual-transformer modality decoupling) are close relatives of existing work (Transfusion, Show-o, LMFusion), and the paper's differentiations from these, while articulated, are more engineering refinements than fundamental advances.

Comparative fairness concerns: Table 2 compares a 2B model against 13B baselines in some rows, and the claimed captioning superiority over Qwen3-VL comes with the caveat that the model trails dedicated 3D captioning models (3D-LLM, PointLLM, ShapeLLM-Omni-7B) on 3D latent inputs. The strong 'understanding' claim in the contributions is thus only partially supported and depends on dataset choices (short MLLM-generated captions, acknowledged in Sec. 4.5).

Some central architectural choices are under-motivated or under-evaluated. The AdaLN negative result is reported with only a loose hypothesis ('additional scaling factors may compromise stability') and no controlled experiment; the ablation of 'standard DiT vs. LLM-style BlockAR' is deferred to this inconclusive subsection rather than directly measured.

The evaluation protocol has gaps: the user study (100 questionnaires, ~2,400 data points) lacks detail on design, raters, and statistical significance; CLIP-based consistency scores are known to be weak proxies for 3D fidelity; and there is no evaluation of text-to-3D separately from image-to-3D despite the framework advertising both conditioning modes.

Reproducibility is uncertain: no code, model weights, or dataset release is mentioned; the dataset curation mixes three sources with ad-hoc filtering (aesthetic score=3 subset), and key details such as exact data mixture proportions and the 3D 'block' structure definition (block size, how latents are grouped into blocks) are not fully specified.

The 'first MLLM supporting end-to-end 3D spatial generation' claim is overclaimed given concurrent/prior unified 3D MLLMs (e.g., ShapeLLM-Omni, SAR3D), even if those rely on coarse proxies; the distinction should be more carefully scoped.

The claimed perception improvement (generation improving 2D-based 3D understanding) is interesting but the evidence is a single captioning benchmark under one training configuration; no control isolates whether the gain stems from 3D latent supervision versus additional multimodal training data or longer training.
